title: Stuffing, sealing & VGM
sceneDesc: Side view of the shipper's premises. A truck brings the container to the loading dock; the cargo is loaded, the container is sealed and the truck is weighed on a weighbridge.

narration.2: Empty {box} at {origin} for a [[live-load]]. My export [[detention]] clock has been running since depot gate-out. [TO VERIFY:v21]
narration.3: Live load at the shipper's dock; carrier-haulage free loading time is typically a few hours, then waiting time is charged. [TO VERIFY:v12]

caption.2: Who hired this truck depends on [[merchant-haulage]] vs [[carrier-haulage]].

1.tank: Here I am at the shipper's site, clean and checked. A hose fills my tank with {cargo}.
1.oog: Here I am at the shipper's site. A crane lowers {cargo} into place — it's too big for a normal box.
1.*: Here I am at the [[shipper]]'s warehouse. The team loads {cargo} into me — that's [[stuffing]] — spreading the weight evenly.

2.reefer: [[stuffing|Stuffing]] of pre-cooled {cargo}: the cargo, not the box, must already be at temperature — a reefer keeps temperature, it doesn't cool warm cargo fast. [TO VERIFY:v56]
2.tank: Filling {cargo} by hose. Tanks must not be over- or under-filled: a minimum and maximum filling level applies to limit surge and expansion. [TO VERIFY:v59]
2.oog: Crane loading of {cargo}, then lashing to the lashing points per the [[ctu-code]]. Dimensions beyond the box make it [[oog]]. [TO VERIFY:v58]
2.*: [[stuffing|Stuffing]] per the [[ctu-code]]: weight spread along my length, voids filled with [[dunnage]], cargo secured. The carrier never sees inside.

3.reefer: Pre-cooled cargo, air flow kept clear (no cargo above the red load line, T-floor uncovered). Stuffing at ambient temperature: unit off or doors closed fast to avoid condensation. [TO VERIFY:v56]
3.tank: Filling ratio within IMDG limits; product compatibility with tank and gaskets checked; placards on all four sides. [TO VERIFY:v59]
3.oog: Lashing calculated for sea forces; overheight/overwidth measured and declared exactly — they drive slot loss and freight. [TO VERIFY:v58]
3.*: CTU Code: centre of gravity within limits, no voids, blocking and bracing. SLAC wording protects the carrier — the shipper owns packing quality. [TO VERIFY:v08]

caption.2: The carrier never sees inside me — hence the [[slac]] clause on the B/L.

1.40FR: I have no doors, so no seal: instead, the lashing is checked and photographed before I leave.
1.*: Doors closed: a numbered [[seal]] goes on my door. If anyone opens me on the way, the broken seal will show it.

2.40FR: Flat racks can't be sealed. The lashing is checked, photographed and documented instead. [TO VERIFY:v58]
2.*: High-security bolt [[seal]] applied ([[iso-17712]] class H). [TO VERIFY:v07] Open the seal record: its number must flow into the next documents.

3.40FR: No seal: pre-shipment survey and photos are the evidence for any later claim.
3.*: Seal number door → SI → B/L → manifest. Customs may cut it and apply their own: the new number must be recorded. [TO VERIFY:v07]

2.tank: DG: [[placard|placards]] on all four sides, DG declaration from the shipper. [TO VERIFY:v25]
2.*: A seal mismatch is a classic trigger for a customs inspection.

narration.1: Before any ship takes me, the carrier needs my [[vgm]]: my total weight, cargo included. No VGM, no loading — it's a worldwide safety rule.
narration.2: Under [[solas]] Ch. VI Reg. 2 the B/L shipper must submit my [[vgm]] before the VGM [[cut-off]]. [TO VERIFY:v01] Open the declaration to see how {vgm} kg was established.
narration.3: VGM: Method 1 (weigh packed box) or Method 2 (certified sum + tare). Estimates are prohibited; the signatory must be authorised by the shipper. [TO VERIFY:v02] [TO VERIFY:v17]
The VGM arrives 3.5 t above the booking estimate, 2 hours before the VGM cut-off. The customer asks you to 'just use the booking weight' because their weighbridge ticket is 'probably wrong'.

text.1: Since 1 July 2016, no packed export container may be loaded on a ship without a verified weight. [TO VERIFY:v01]
text.2: After the MSC Napoli was beached in 2007, about 20% of 660 boxes checked were more than 3 t off their declared weight. [TO VERIFY:v09]

body.1: The company sending the goods — here, {origin}. It packs the container itself.
body.2: In the SOLAS sense, the shipper is the party named as shipper on the B/L — not necessarily the factory. Under {incoterm}: {vgmBy}. [TO VERIFY:v03]
Merchant haulage: the shipper or forwarder hires the haulier. Carrier haulage: the carrier arranges and invoices it, with free loading time then waiting-time charges. [TO VERIFY:v12]

reefer.1: {cargo}, kept at {setPoint}. The cold chain must never break.
reefer.2: Set point {setPoint}. Cargo must be pre-cooled; reefers maintain temperature but have limited pull-down capacity. [TO VERIFY:v56]

tank.1: {cargo}. Dangerous goods follow strict international rules.
tank.2: Class 3 flammable liquid: IMDG declaration, placards, segregation, emergency information. [TO VERIFY:v59]

oog.1: {cargo}: too big or too heavy for a normal container.
oog.2: Exact dimensions, weight and centre of gravity must be declared; overheight costs slots on board. [TO VERIFY:v58]

*.1: {cargo}. Good packing protects them during more than a month at sea.
*.2: Watch for condensation ('container rain'): desiccants and dry pallets help. Wooden pallets must usually meet [[ispm15]]. [TO VERIFY:v24]

body.2: The [[ctu-code]] gives guidance on load distribution: a heavy end is dangerous to lift and to drive. [TO VERIFY:v08]

body.1: A single-use, numbered lock that can only be removed by cutting it. Its number goes into the shipping documents: a broken or different seal shows that someone opened me.
A flat rack has no doors to seal. The chains and straps holding the cargo are checked and photographed instead.
body.2: Lashing must withstand sea forces (rolling, pitching). Photos and a survey report are the evidence if a claim arises. [TO VERIFY:v58]

body.1: The orange-red diamond tells everyone the tank holds a flammable liquid (class 3).
body.2: [[placard|Placards]] on all sides, UN number displayed, DG declaration and container packing certificate from the shipper. [TO VERIFY:v25] [TO VERIFY:v59]

body.1: VGM = my own empty weight ([[tare]]) + everything inside me. It must reach the carrier before the VGM deadline, or I stay on the quay.
My maximum weight ({mgm} kg) and my empty weight ({tare} kg) are painted on my door. [TO VERIFY:v53]
body.2: MGM, tare and payload, plus the [[csc-plate]]. Use the actual markings of the unit, not a typical value. [TO VERIFY:v05]

body.1: A giant scale for trucks: weigh the loaded truck, then subtract the truck's own weight.
body.2: Certified and calibrated per national rules (Method 1). Road limits apply too, e.g. 44 t gross for a 5-axle combination in France. [TO VERIFY:v02] [TO VERIFY:v13]

points.1: Owner code + serial + check digit (ISO 6346). It identifies me on every document and gate message. [TO VERIFY:v32]
points.2: Must be identical on the door, in the [[si]] and on the [[bl]]. If customs cuts it and applies its own, the new number must be recorded.
points.3: Class H high-security seal per [[iso-17712]] — the usual standard for international shipments. [TO VERIFY:v07]

2.prompt: Where must this seal number appear next?

options.text: In the shipping instructions (SI), then on the B/L
Only on the truck driver's delivery note
options.fb: The road note is not where the carrier and customs look.

options.text: On the VGM declaration instead of the B/L
options.fb: The VGM is about weight; the seal belongs in the SI and B/L.

options.text: Nowhere — the seal itself is the proof
options.fb: A seal proves nothing unless its number is recorded and compared.

2.explain: Door → SI → B/L → manifest. Terminals and customs compare the door with the documents; a mismatch triggers checks and L/C discrepancies.

3.prompt: Origin customs inspects the box after stuffing and applies their seal CU-0099. The SI already shows {sealNo}. What is correct?

options.text: Update the SI/B/L draft and the manifest data with the new seal number before issuance and filing
Keep {sealNo}: the shipper's seal is the contractual one
options.fb: The door now carries CU-0099; documents must match the door.

options.text: Ask the terminal to replace CU-0099 with a copy of {sealNo}
options.fb: Nobody may re-seal with a fake number.

options.text: Nothing: customs seals are never checked at destination
options.fb: Destination customs and the consignee check the seal against the documents.

3.explain: Seal changes must be documented; otherwise the box risks a hold at destination and the carrier's position in a shortage claim is weakened.

vgm.title: VGM declaration
vgm.heading: VERIFIED GROSS MASS DECLARATION
vgm.sub: SOLAS Ch. VI Reg. 2 · fictional example

rows.label: Method
rows.value: Method 1 — packed container weighed on a certified weighbridge

points.1: Method 1 weighs the packed container; Method 2 adds certified weights of all contents to the tare. Estimates are never allowed. [TO VERIFY:v02]
points.2: {vgm} kg = cargo and packaging {cargoKg} kg + tare {tare} kg. Both methods must give the same result. (Illustrative figures.)
points.3: Signed by a person duly authorised by the B/L shipper, sent before the VGM cut-off by portal, [[edi]] (VERMAS) or platform. [TO VERIFY:v17] [TO VERIFY:v16]

2.prompt: Which weights does the VGM include?

options.text: Cargo, packaging, pallets, dunnage and the container's tare
Cargo and its packaging only
options.fb: That's closer to the B/L gross weight — it excludes the tare.

options.text: Everything inside, but not the tare
options.fb: The crane lifts the container too: the tare is included.

options.text: The packed container plus the truck and chassis
options.fb: The truck is weighed, then subtracted (Method 1).

2.explain: The VGM is the packed container as it will be lifted: everything inside plus the tare. The B/L gross weight, by contrast, excludes the tare.

3.prompt: The shipper uses Method 2. Which practice is NOT acceptable?

options.text: Estimating dunnage and pallet weight from last month's average shipment
Using the tare marked on the container door
options.fb: Method 2 explicitly uses the marked tare.

options.text: Weighing each package type on calibrated scales and adding them up
options.fb: That is Method 2 when the procedure is certified/approved.

options.text: Using manufacturer-sealed package weights clearly marked on the packages
options.fb: Accepted under the IMO guidelines for sealed packages, depending on national rules.

3.explain: Method 2 requires actual (certified/approved) weights of all contents, including packing and securing material; estimates are not allowed. [TO VERIFY:v02]

documents: **Booking confirmation** — cut-offs for VGM, SI and port.
**[[eir|EIR]]** from empty pick-up — the box's condition before stuffing.
**Packing list** — the shipper's own document; it feeds the SI.
**VGM declaration** — portal, EDI VERMAS or platform. [TO VERIFY:v16]

documents.text: **DG declaration + container packing certificate** — dangerous goods only. [TO VERIFY:v25]

costs: **Detention** — export clock from empty gate-out to full gate-in. [TO VERIFY:v21]
**Waiting time** — carrier haulage beyond the free loading time. [TO VERIFY:v12]
**VGM fees** — some carriers charge for late, amended or manual VGM. [TO VERIFY:v12]
**Weighing and seal fees** — where applicable. [TO VERIFY:v12]
risks: **Missed VGM cut-off** → shut out, rolled to the next sailing (+7 days on a weekly service).
**Wrong VGM** → amendment fees; overweight boxes can be refused or break road limits. [TO VERIFY:v13]
**Seal mismatch** → customs or terminal check and delay.
**Poor stowage** → cargo claims, which the [[slac]] clause puts on the shipper.
jobs: **Documentation** — VGM reception, consistency with the SI.
**Vessel planning** — needs VGMs to build a safe stowage plan.

incoNote.EXW: Under EXW, the goods were delivered at the seller's door: loading is at the buyer's risk unless agreed otherwise, and the buyer's forwarder owes the VGM.
incoNote.*: The B/L shipper owes the VGM — under {incoterm}: {vgmBy}.

1: Goods are loaded ('stuffed') at the shipper's premises — the carrier doesn't see inside.
A numbered seal proves the container hasn't been opened.
No VGM, no loading: the total weight must reach the carrier before the deadline.
2: Stuffing follows the CTU Code; the SLAC clause reflects that the carrier relies on the shipper.
The seal number flows door → SI → B/L; mismatches trigger inspections.
SOLAS VGM: two methods, signed, before the VGM cut-off; missing VGM = shut-out.
The Incoterm decides who is B/L shipper — and therefore who owes the VGM.
3: The VGM is a legal declaration by the shipper; the carrier must not replace it with an estimate.
Seal changes after inspections must be documented end to end.
Reefer, DG and OOG stuffing have their own rules: pre-cooling, filling ratios, lashing.

1.prompt: I'm stuffed, sealed and my total weight is known. What happens next?
1.hint: Where am I right now — and what does the carrier need before a ship can take me?

options.text: A truck takes me to the port terminal, and my VGM is sent to the carrier before the deadline.
options.confirm: Right. I travel to the port terminal (that's 'pre-carriage'), and the carrier must have my VGM before the cut-off. Under {incoterm}, this trip is paid by {preBy}.

options.text: I'm lifted straight onto the ship.
options.why: I'm still at the warehouse, far from the sea. I first have to reach the port and enter the terminal.
options.realLife: A box without a VGM, or not on the loading list, stays on the quay and waits for the next ship — usually a week later.

options.text: I'm delivered to the customer at destination.
options.why: I haven't left {pol} yet! Export customs, loading, the voyage and import customs all come first.
options.realLife: Customs on both sides must clear the goods, and the carrier only releases me to the right party.
options.whenRight: That's step 10 — near the end of the journey.

2.prompt: Stuffed, sealed, VGM determined (Method 1). What happens next?

options.text: Pre-carriage to the export terminal; the VGM reaches the carrier before the VGM cut-off, and the SI follows before the documentation cut-off.
options.confirm: Correct. The full box moves to the terminal before the port cut-off, while VGM and SI meet their own cut-offs — sequence and timings vary by carrier and port. [TO VERIFY:v20]

options.text: The carrier issues the Bill of Lading now that the seal number and weights are known.
options.why: The B/L is drafted from the SI, not yet submitted — and a 'shipped on board' B/L needs the box to be loaded.
options.realLife: An early B/L certifies something untrue: claims, L/C discrepancies, amendment fees.
options.whenRight: A 'received for shipment' B/L can follow the carrier's receipt of the goods, on the basis of the SI.

options.text: Load the container on the first available vessel; the VGM can follow with the manifest.
options.why: SOLAS: a packed container without a VGM must not be loaded. [TO VERIFY:v01]
options.realLife: Shut-out: rolled to the next sailing, extra storage and detention.

options.text: Return the laden container to the empty depot so the carrier can check weight and seal.
options.why: Depots handle empty equipment. Weight and seal are the shipper's responsibility.
options.realLife: The depot refuses it: an extra trip and a possibly missed cut-off.
options.whenRight: Under carrier haulage via an inland depot named in the booking, laden boxes can be received inland — not at the empty depot.

3.prompt: Case: the VGM is 3.5 t above the booking estimate; the customer asks you to use the booking weight instead. What should you do?

options.text: Refuse: only the shipper's verified VGM can be used. If the shipper doubts it, they must re-verify and submit a corrected VGM before the cut-off.
options.confirm: Right. The VGM is the shipper's legal declaration; the carrier may not substitute an estimate. A re-weigh is possible, but a corrected VGM must still arrive before cut-off or the box is shut out. [TO VERIFY:v01] [TO VERIFY:v03]

options.text: Enter the booking weight in the system — it's what the customer says.
options.why: A booking weight is an estimate, not a verified mass.
options.realLife: Wrong weights endanger stowage and stability; the carrier becomes party to a misdeclaration.

options.text: Accept the higher VGM but load the box anyway even if it exceeds road limits.
options.why: Road limits concern the haulier; the issue here is which weight is valid.
options.realLife: Overweight on the road can mean fines and a stopped truck. [TO VERIFY:v13]
options.whenRight: Accepting the VGM is right; ignoring road limits is not.

options.text: Average the two weights to be safe.
options.why: There's no such thing as an 'average VGM'.
options.realLife: An invented weight is a misdeclaration with liability for whoever enters it.
